lesson.title: Why the Second Electron Never Comes Cheap
lesson.summary: Successive ionization energies track the energy cost of removing electrons one after another from the same atom, and the huge jumps between them reveal exactly how many valence electrons an atom has.
lesson.body:
Removing one electron from an atom is only the beginning of the story. Once that first electron is gone, the atom becomes a positively charged ion, and removing a second electron means pulling a negative charge away from a particle that is now more positive overall. The remaining electrons are held more tightly because there are fewer of them spreading out the same nuclear charge, and the ion itself exerts an extra pull because of its positive charge. As a result, each successive ionization energy, IE1, IE2, IE3, and so on, is always larger than the one before it. This is the same nucleus to electron attraction that defines ionization energy in general, just applied over and over to a shrinking, increasingly positive electron cloud.

What makes successive ionization energies so useful is not that they increase, but how unevenly they increase. As long as you are removing electrons from the same principal energy level, the jump from one ionization energy to the next is modest, typically two to three times larger. But the moment you try to remove an electron from a full, lower shell, the jump becomes enormous, often ten times larger or more. That happens because core electrons sit much closer to the nucleus, are barely shielded from it, and are part of an especially stable filled shell configuration.

Sodium makes this pattern unmistakable. Sodium's electron configuration is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1, with a single valence electron in the 3s orbital. Its first ionization energy is only 496 kilojoules per mole, reflecting how loosely that lone 3s electron is held. But the second ionization energy jumps to 4562 kilojoules per mole, more than nine times higher, because that electron has to come out of the full, tightly bound 2p6 core. Every ionization energy after that keeps climbing, IE3 is about 6912 kilojoules per mole and IE4 about 9543 kilojoules per mole, but none of those later jumps come close to the size of the first one, because all of them are pulling electrons from that same stable core.

The same logic applies to any element, and it lets you read an atom's number of valence electrons directly off a table of successive ionization energies. Magnesium, with two valence electrons in its 3s2 configuration, shows a modest jump from IE1, 738 kilojoules per mole, to IE2, 1451 kilojoules per mole, but then a massive jump to IE3, 7733 kilojoules per mole, once the core is breached. Aluminum, with three valence electrons, shows gradual increases through IE1, IE2, and IE3, and only slams into a huge jump at IE4, around 11577 kilojoules per mole. In each case, the big jump lands exactly one step after the number of valence electrons is exhausted.

This pattern is one of the most direct pieces of experimental evidence for shell structure itself. Chemists did not simply assume atoms have electrons arranged in discrete shells around a core, successive ionization energy data, gathered element by element, showed exactly where those shells begin and end. It also explains why elements almost always form ions with predictable charges: sodium loses one electron to form Na+ and stops, because losing a second would mean paying an enormous energy price to break into a stable, noble gas like core.
